title: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
hook: a hunter drags a snake to a grieving mother so she can watch it die, and she tells him to let it go
carry: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
tomorrow: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)

segments.voice: Yesterday in Shanti and Anushasana, a pigeon honored the hunter who trapped his mate, and the hunter laid down his nets. Did you give someone an unexpected welcome? Today, the Anushasana opens. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

After all of Bhishma's teaching, Yudhishthira is still stuck in the same place. I caused all this, he says. I'm the reason you're lying on those arrows. So when the Anushasana Parva opens, Bhishma answers him with a story about blame. An old woman named Gautami finds her son dead. A snake has bitten him. A hunter, Arjunaka, catches the snake, ties it with a cord, and drags it to her. Tell me how to kill it, he says. Fire, or cut it to pieces? Either is fine with me. Today, what Gautami answers.
screen: `"I CAUSED ALL THIS."` → `A BOY BITTEN BY A SNAKE.` → `"HOW SHALL I KILL IT?"`

segments.voice: Gautami says: let it go. Killing it won't bring my son back, and it won't make me any less sad. The hunter argues; surely the guilty should pay. And then the snake speaks up. Don't blame me, it says. I didn't act on my own. Death sent me. And Death, Mrityu, appears. Don't blame me either, says Death. I was directed by Time. Then Time itself, Kala, arrives. And Time says: none of us is the real cause. The boy's own past actions brought him here, his karma. We were only the instruments. Gautami listens, and accepts it. The hunter lets the snake go. Death and Time depart. That's a strange chain, and Bhishma means it to be. Each one in the line points at the next, and the chain ends not in a villain but in the long working of actions and their results. Now look at who Bhishma is telling it to. Yudhishthira is sure he's the snake. He believes the deaths are on him alone. Bhishma is saying, gently, that you are one link in something much longer, and you are not the whole of it. This isn't permission to stop caring. It's a way out of the kind of guilt that eats a person alive and helps nobody. And notice who sees it first. Not the warrior, not the king. A grieving old mother, the one with every reason to want revenge, is the one who says let it go. Anushasana means instruction, and its opening lesson, in this story, is about where blame stops.
screen: `"LET IT GO"` · `THE SNAKE, DEATH, AND TIME` · `THE CHAIN ENDS IN KARMA` · then, large: `YOU ARE NOT THE WHOLE OF IT`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your jaw soften. Bring to mind something you still blame yourself for. Breathe in, and see your part in it honestly. Breathe out, and let the other causes come into view: other people, timing, things nobody chose. You don't have to excuse anything. Just let the picture be its true size. If you pray, you can bring that weight into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shanti and Anushasana. Today, the Anushasana's opening story: Gautami, the snake, Death and Time, and a mother who says let it go.

Your line: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows. Today, when you're sure one person is to blame, look for one more link in the chain. Tomorrow, Bhishma lets go. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: The story of Gautami, the snake, Death and Time is retold by Hindu teachers when they speak of karma and of letting go of revenge, and it stands at the opening of the Anushasana Parva.

match.prompt: the chain of blame — tap the pairs.

myth: Gautami asked the hunter to kill the snake
she told him to let it go; killing it wouldn't bring her son back.
Death blamed Time for the boy's death
Death said it was directed by Time, and Time pointed to the boy's karma.
Bhishma tells the story to Yudhishthira about his guilt
Yudhishthira believed the deaths were on him alone.

fork.setup: you're Gautami. your son lies dead, and a hunter holds the snake that bit him, asking how you want it killed. what do you say?
fork.reveal: she says let it go, since killing it won't bring her son back, and then the snake, Death and Time each speak.

original.note: instruction: the name of the book that opens with Gautami's story.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone always has to be the one to blame.
what it means: the snake, Death and Time each point onward, and the chain ends in karma.
what a scholar hears: Bhishma uses the story to free Yudhishthira from a guilt that claims too much, not to excuse wrongdoing.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, the opening story of Gautami, the fowler Arjunaka, the serpent, Mrityu and Kala

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli the opening of the Anushasana Parva: Yudhishthira's self-blame, Gautami, the fowler Arjunaka, the serpent, Mrityu (Death) and Kala (Time), and the conclusion in the boy's karma.
Confirm the hunter's offer of fire or cutting as methods.
Theological framing of karma as the end of the chain: a Keeper may want to add nuance (Kala's role, or the teaching that all act under Time).
Audit: 'where blame really stops' softened to 'in this story, where blame stops' so the narrator does not assert the doctrine.
